chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Sovereign Debt Actually Is

lessons.title: Sovereign Debt in Numbers: Debt-to-GDP, External vs Domestic, and Why the Mix Matters

children.text: You now know why governments borrow and who actually lends to them. This lesson gets into the numbers analysts, rating agencies, and financial news actually quote, starting with the one everybody leads with: debt-to-GDP. By the end of this lesson you should be able to look at two countries with similar debt-to-GDP ratios and explain why one is in a genuine crisis and the other is not, which is exactly the situation Japan and Sri Lanka present.

markDefs.definition: Total government debt outstanding, without subtracting any financial assets the government itself holds. This is the figure most commonly quoted and is what India's Centre and general government ratios refer to.

children.text: Debt-to-GDP divides the total stock of outstanding government debt by the country's annual economic output. India's Centre debt-to-GDP sits at roughly 57%, and its general government figure, Centre plus states, at roughly 80%. What the ratio is really asking is: relative to the size of the economy that has to eventually service this debt through taxation, how large is the pile? Most headline figures you see quoted, including these, are

, not net debt. Net debt would subtract the government's own financial assets, like its forex reserves or holdings in public sector banks, from the total. India, like most countries, is usually discussed in gross terms, so keep in mind that the number you are looking at is the full liability side only.

body.text: Do not compare two countries' debt-to-GDP ratios and stop there. A 100% ratio means something completely different for a country borrowing in its own currency from its own citizens than it does for a country borrowing in dollars from foreign fund managers. The ratio tells you the size of the debt. It tells you almost nothing, on its own, about whether that debt is actually risky.

children.text: The Mix: External vs Domestic, Short vs Long

You saw in the last lesson that India's government debt is overwhelmingly domestic and rupee-denominated. The second dimension that matters just as much is maturity: how soon does the debt need to be refinanced? A government that has to roll over 40% of its debt every year is far more exposed to a sudden change in investor sentiment than one whose debt is spread out over decades. This is why debt managers do not just care about how much is owed, they care intensely about the maturity profile of what is owed.

markDefs.definition: The average time remaining until a portfolio of bonds matures, weighted by the size of each bond. A longer weighted average maturity means less of the debt needs to be refinanced in any given year, reducing rollover risk.

children.text: India's public debt managers, the RBI and the Finance Ministry's Public Debt Management Cell, actively manage this. The

of India's outstanding G-Secs is around 11 to 12 years, deliberately kept long through issuance choices, including bonds running out to 30 or even 50 years. Compare that to a country forced to borrow mostly in short-term instruments because investors will not commit long-term money to it: it must return to the market again and again, and every one of those returns is a fresh opportunity for lenders to demand a higher rate or simply refuse to lend, which is exactly the dynamic behind many sovereign debt crises.

children.text: The Part Most Headlines Miss: Contingent Liabilities

markDefs.definition: An obligation that only becomes an actual government liability if a specific future event occurs, such as a guaranteed loan going bad. Not counted in headline debt-to-GDP figures unless and until it is called.

children.text: The 57% and 80% figures quoted earlier do not tell the whole story. Governments routinely take on

: guarantees extended to public sector companies, state electricity distribution companies (discoms), or infrastructure special purpose vehicles, so those entities can borrow more cheaply on the strength of the government's backing. As long as the guaranteed borrower keeps paying, none of this shows up in the headline debt-to-GDP number. If it defaults, the guarantee gets called, and the liability lands squarely on the government's own balance sheet overnight. India's discom debt and periodic state government guarantee schemes, along with off-budget borrowings routed through entities like the Food Corporation of India in past years, are the most commonly cited domestic examples of this blind spot.

body.title: The Hidden Liability
body.scenario: An analyst compares two Indian states. State X reports a headline debt-to-GSDP ratio of 25%. State Y reports a headline ratio of 22%, appearing safer. However, State Y has also guaranteed Rs 40,000 crore of borrowing by its state power distribution company, which is losing money every year and increasingly relies on the state government to service its own debt.
body.prompt: Why might State Y actually be the riskier of the two, despite its lower headline debt ratio?
body.modelAnswer: State Y's headline ratio excludes the discom's guaranteed debt because it is a contingent liability, not direct state government debt. But if the loss-making discom cannot service that debt itself, the guarantee will very likely be called, and Rs 40,000 crore would land on State Y's own balance sheet. An analyst who only looks at the headline 22% is missing a liability that could push State Y's effective debt burden well above State X's, which has no such guarantee hanging over it. This is exactly why sovereign and sub-sovereign risk analysis has to look past the headline ratio into guarantees, off-budget borrowing, and the health of guaranteed entities.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Japan's debt-to-GDP ratio, at around 260%, is far higher than Sri Lanka's was when it defaulted in 2022, at around 100%. What best explains why Japan has not faced a debt crisis?
options: Japan's debt-to-GDP figure is calculated using a different, more favourable formula
Japan's debt is mostly held domestically in its own currency, unlike Sri Lanka's large foreign-currency commercial debt
Japan does not actually have to repay its government debt
The IMF does not track Japan's debt levels
body.explanation: The composition of debt, not just its size relative to GDP, determines how dangerous it is. Japan's debt is almost entirely yen-denominated and held by Japanese banks, insurers, and the Bank of Japan, so there is no currency mismatch and little risk of foreign investors suddenly refusing to roll it over. Sri Lanka's debt included a large share of foreign-currency commercial borrowing, including dollar Eurobonds, owed to investors who could and did lose confidence and pull back, precipitating the 2022 default.

body.text: Debt-to-GDP tells you the size of the mountain. Currency composition, maturity profile, who holds the debt, and contingent liabilities tell you whether the mountain is stable. Never read the first number without asking about the other three.

children.text: The next lesson puts all of this together into a single, detailed case study of India's own borrowing programme, walking through how an actual G-Sec auction works, how the RBI manages India's debt profile in practice, and what retail investors can now access directly through RBI Retail Direct.

points: Debt-to-GDP compares total outstanding government debt to annual economic output; most quoted figures, including India's, are gross debt, not net of the government's own financial assets.
Two countries can share a similar debt-to-GDP ratio and face completely different risk levels. Composition matters as much as the headline number.

Currency denomination (domestic vs foreign) and the investor base (captive domestic vs flighty foreign) are the two biggest drivers of why similar ratios produce different outcomes, as Japan versus Sri Lanka shows.
Maturity profile matters too: a longer weighted average maturity, like India's roughly 11 to 12 years, means less debt needs refinancing in any given year, reducing rollover risk.
Headline debt-to-GDP figures typically exclude contingent liabilities, like government guarantees to PSUs or discoms, which can turn into real government debt overnight if called.

body.text: The debt-to-GDP ratios, maturity figures, and country comparisons in this lesson are approximate and drawn from recent RBI, IMF, and government data. These figures move with each fiscal year and data revision. Verify current numbers against the RBI's Public Debt Management Report, the IMF's World Economic Outlook database, or the relevant country's finance ministry before using them in analysis or advice.
